title: Myself, each other, and whose is it anyway?
title_target: De har varit gifta med varandra i femtio år.
goal: Go beyond the basic reflexive verbs: use *sig själv* and *varandra*, choose correctly between *sin* and *hans/hennes* in long sentences, and say "my own" with *egen*.
bekal: you can tell *sig* (part of the verb) from *sig själv* (a real "himself") and from *varandra* (each other)
you can apply the subject rule for *sin/sitt/sina* in main clauses, *att*-clauses and after *be någon att*
you can use *egen/eget/egna* and *själv* ("by myself") naturally
wave: Go back to Svenska 102, Unit 7: say the reflexive verbs from that dialogue (*sätta sig, känna sig, skynda sig, gifta sig*) with every person — *jag sätter mig, du sätter dig … de sätter sig* — then make three sentences of your own with *sig själv* from this unit.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Teamdagen
dialogs.intro: Karin has booked a team day for the whole office in a conference room at Lindholmen. Coffee, cinnamon buns, and an exercise that makes Mattias groan: introducing a colleague to the group.

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Välkomna till teamdagen! Idag ska vi lära känna varandra lite bättre.
lines.id: Welcome to team day! Today we're going to get to know each other a bit better.
lines.literal: welcome to team-day-the! today shall we learn know each-other little better.

lines.speaker: Mattias:
lines.text: Men vi känner ju redan varandra. Leila och jag har jobbat ihop i sju år.
lines.id: But we already know each other. Leila and I have worked together for seven years.
lines.literal: but we know you-know already each-other. Leila and I have worked together in seven years.

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Ni två, ja. Men Dian har bara varit här i två månader. Första övningen: presentera en kollega, inte er själva.
lines.id: You two, yes. But Dian has only been here for two months. First exercise: introduce a colleague, not yourselves.
lines.literal: you two, yes. but Dian has only been here in two months. first exercise-the: present a colleague, not yourselves.

lines.speaker: Leila:
lines.text: Okej, jag börjar. Det här är Mattias. Han tänker mest på sig själv och sin kaffemaskin.
lines.id: OK, I'll start. This is Mattias. He mostly thinks about himself and his coffee machine.
lines.literal: okay, I begin. this here is Mattias. he thinks most on himself and his-own coffee-machine.

lines.speaker: Mattias:
lines.text: Det är inte sant! Jag köpte en egen maskin så att ni andra skulle slippa vänta.
lines.id: That's not true! I bought my own machine so the rest of you wouldn't have to wait.
lines.literal: it is not true! I bought an own machine so that you others should escape wait.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Det stämmer. Han lärde mig att göra espresso på min första dag.
lines.id: That's right. He taught me how to make espresso on my first day.
lines.literal: it tallies. he taught me to make espresso on my first day.

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Fint. Mattias, nu är det din tur att presentera Dian.
lines.id: Nice. Mattias, now it's your turn to introduce Dian.
lines.literal: fine. Mattias, now is it your turn to present Dian.

lines.speaker: Mattias:
lines.text: Dian kommer från Indonesien. Hon har berättat att hennes familj aldrig har sett snö.
lines.id: Dian comes from Indonesia. She's told us her family has never seen snow.
lines.literal: Dian comes from Indonesia. she has told that her family never has seen snow.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Det stämmer. Men nu har min lillebror köpt sin första vinterjacka — han ska hälsa på mig i december.
lines.id: That's right. But now my little brother has bought his first winter jacket — he's coming to visit me in December.
lines.literal: it tallies. but now has my little-brother bought his-own first winter-jacket — he shall greet on me in December.

lines.speaker: Leila:
lines.text: Vad roligt! Då måste ni gå på julmarknaden på Liseberg.
lines.id: How fun! Then you two have to go to the Christmas market at Liseberg.
lines.literal: what fun! then must you go on Christmas-market-the on Liseberg.

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Bra jobbat, allihop. Nu ska ni sitta i par och prata med varandra om era egna mål för våren.
lines.id: Well done, everybody. Now you'll sit in pairs and talk to each other about your own goals for the spring.
lines.literal: good worked, all-up. now shall you sit in pairs and talk with each-other about your own goals for spring-the.

lines.speaker: Mattias:
lines.text: Får jag välja min egen partner?
lines.id: Can I choose my own partner?
lines.literal: may I choose my own partner?

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Nej. Du jobbar med Dian, och Leila jobbar med mig.
lines.id: No. You're working with Dian, and Leila's working with me.
lines.literal: no. you work with Dian, and Leila works with me.

notes: **Lära känna varandra** — *varandra* (**vah-RAHN-drah**) is "each other", and it is the only way to say it with most verbs: *vi känner varandra*, *de hjälper varandra*, *prata med varandra*. Don't use *sig* for "each other" — *de känner sig* means "they feel" (as in *de känner sig trötta*), a completely different verb.

**Presentera en kollega, inte er själva** — *själv* adds a real "-self" when the person is an object in contrast to someone else. It agrees in number: *mig själv, dig själv, sig själv*, but *oss själva, er själva, sig själva*. Karin speaks to the whole group, so *er själva*.

**Han tänker mest på sig själv och sin kaffemaskin** — after a preposition, Swedes almost always say *sig själv*, not just *sig*: *tänka på sig själv*, *prata med sig själv*, *vara arg på sig själv*. And *sin* (**sin**) = "his own", because it points back to *han*, the subject of the same clause.

**En egen maskin** — *egen* (**EH-gen**) means "own" and agrees like an adjective: *en egen maskin*, *ett eget rum*, *egna mål*. After a possessive the noun stays indefinite and *egen* takes the long form for *ett*-words and plurals: *min egen partner*, *mitt eget rum*, *era egna mål*. English needs "my own"; Swedish can even say *en egen* with no possessive at all.

**Hon har berättat att hennes familj…** — why *hennes* and not *sin*? Because *hennes familj* is itself the **subject** of the *att*-clause, and *sin* can never be part of a subject. *Sin* only points back to a subject; it never sits inside one.

**Min lillebror har köpt sin första vinterjacka** — here *sin* is right: the subject is *min lillebror*, and the jacket is his. Liseberg, the big amusement park in the middle of Göteborg, turns into a Christmas market every winter — a classic first trip for visitors who have never seen snow.

grammars.title: sig, sig själv, varandra — and the -s verbs
body: Swedish has three different tools where English uses "-self" and "each other". Keep them apart:

head: Form
When
Example
rows: part of a reflexive verb; no real "self" is meant
a real object, often in contrast with others or after a preposition
Han tänker bara på **sig själv**. Jag tvättade **mig själv**, inte barnen.
each other — two or more people doing it to one another
a short way to say *varandra* with a few common verbs
by oneself, oneself (emphatic), not an object

after: Compare: *Han tvättar sig* (he washes — the normal morning routine) with *Han tvättar sig själv* (he washes himself, as opposed to someone else). The second needs a reason to exist.
The possessive of *varandra* is ***varandras***: *De lånar varandras kläder* = They borrow each other's clothes.
Only a handful of verbs make the reciprocal with *-s*: *träffas, ses, hörs, kramas, pussas, slåss, mötas, hjälpas åt*. For all others, use *varandra*.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Guldbröllopet
dialogs.intro: A Saturday in October. Oskar's grandparents are celebrating their golden wedding anniversary at their house in Kungälv, just north of the city, and Oskar has brought Dian along. The garden is full of relatives, and there is a very large cake.

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Där är farmor och farfar. De har varit gifta med varandra i femtio år idag.
lines.id: There are Grandma and Grandpa. They've been married to each other for fifty years today.
lines.literal: there are father's-mother and father's-father. they have been married with each-other in fifty years today.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Femtio år! Hur träffades de?
lines.id: Fifty years! How did they meet?
lines.literal: fifty years! how met-each-other they?

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: På en dans i Kungälv 1975. Farfar säger att han bjöd upp henne, men farmor säger att hon bjöd upp honom.
lines.id: At a dance in Kungälv in 1975. Grandpa says he asked her to dance, but Grandma says she asked him.
lines.literal: on a dance in Kungälv 1975. grandpa says that he invited up her, but grandma says that she invited up him.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Och vem har rätt?
lines.id: And who's right?
lines.literal: and who has right?

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Ingen vet. De bråkar fortfarande om det, men de är galna i varandra.
lines.id: Nobody knows. They still argue about it, but they're crazy about each other.
lines.literal: nobody knows. they quarrel still about it, but they are crazy in each-other.

lines.speaker: Oskars farmor:
lines.text: Hej, du måste vara Dian! Oskar har berättat så mycket om dig.
lines.id: Hi, you must be Dian! Oskar has told me so much about you.
lines.literal: hi, you must be Dian! Oskar has told so much about you.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Grattis på guldbröllopet! Vilken fin fest.
lines.id: Congratulations on your golden wedding! What a lovely party.
lines.literal: congrats on gold-wedding-the! which fine party.

lines.speaker: Oskars farmor:
lines.text: Tack, kära du. Vi har bott i vårt eget hus här sedan 1980, så det kändes rätt att fira hemma.
lines.id: Thank you, dear. We've lived in our own house here since 1980, so it felt right to celebrate at home.
lines.literal: thanks, dear you. we have lived in our own house here since 1980, so it felt right to celebrate at-home.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Vad är hemligheten bakom ett så långt äktenskap?
lines.id: What's the secret of such a long marriage?
lines.literal: what is secret-the behind a so long marriage?

lines.speaker: Oskars farmor:
lines.text: Man ska ta hand om varandra — och ibland om sig själv. Farfar har sin båt och jag har min kör.
lines.id: You have to take care of each other — and sometimes of yourself. Grandpa has his boat and I have my choir.
lines.literal: one shall take hand about each-other — and sometimes about oneself. grandpa has his-own boat and I have my choir.

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Och farfar säger att du alltid får din vilja igenom.
lines.id: And Grandpa says you always get your way.
lines.literal: and grandpa says that you always get your will through.

lines.speaker: Oskars farmor:
lines.text: Det är bara för att jag har rätt! Ta nu en bit tårta själv, Dian, innan farfar äter upp allt.
lines.id: That's only because I'm right! Now help yourself to a piece of cake, Dian, before Grandpa eats it all.
lines.literal: it is only because I have right! take now a piece cake self, Dian, before grandpa eats up all.

notes: **Gifta med varandra** — *vara gift med* = to be married to. The reflexive verb from Svenska 102, *gifta sig* (to get married), describes the event: *De gifte sig 1976.* The participle *gift* describes the state: *De har varit gifta i femtio år.*

**Hur träffades de?** — *träffas* is one of the few verbs with a reciprocal *-s*: *träffades* = met each other. *Hur träffade de varandra?* says the same thing at greater length. Notice the past form *träffades*: the *-s* simply goes on after the normal past ending.

**Farfar säger att han bjöd upp henne** — *bjuda upp* (**BYÜ-dah ÜP**) is "to ask (someone) to dance" — a particle verb from the strong family *bjuda – bjöd – bjudit* of Unit 2. No reflexive here: *han* and *henne* are two different people.

**Vårt eget hus** — *hus* is an *ett*-word, so after the possessive *vårt* we get *eget*, and the noun stays indefinite: *vårt eget hus*, never *vårt egna huset*. (You will hear *mitt egna rum* in casual speech, but *mitt eget rum* is the standard.)

**Man ska ta hand om varandra — och ibland om sig själv** — the reflexive of *man* (one, you) is *sig*: *Man måste tänka på sig själv ibland.* And *sin/sitt/sina* follows too: *Man ska älska sin familj.* *Farfar har sin båt* = his own boat, because *farfar* is the subject.

**Ta en bit tårta själv** — *själv* without *sig* means "yourself, by yourself": help yourself, don't wait to be served. *Jag har bakat den själv* = I baked it myself. A *tårta* (**TOH-tah**) is a layered cream cake; a *kaka* is a simple cake or a cookie.

grammars.title: sin or hans? The subject rule, clause by clause
body: *Sin/sitt/sina* means "his/her/its/their **own**" and points back to the **subject of its own clause**. In a long sentence, every clause has its own subject — so find the right one before you choose.

head: Sentence
Whose?
Why
rows: Farmor säger att farfar har **sin** båt.
Farmor säger att farfar har **hennes** bil.
*hennes bror* is the subject itself — *sin* is impossible
Karin bad Dian att ta med **sin** dator.
Dian is the one who will *ta med* → the hidden subject

after: The trick in the fifth row: after *be någon att*, *hjälpa någon att*, *låta någon* etc., the person asked is the "doer" of the infinitive, so *sin* points to that person.

English "his" is ambiguous in *He said that John had lost his keys*. Swedish isn't: *…att John hade tappat **sina** nycklar* (John's own) vs *…att John hade tappat **hans** nycklar* (the first man's). This is why Swedes find the rule so useful.

blocks.text: Three small words do the work English shares between "own", "-self" and "alone". Learn the forms as a set:

Watch the difference between **själv** and **ensam**: *Jag gjorde det själv* means nobody helped; *Jag var ensam* means nobody was there — and can sound lonely. *Jag bor själv* is also common in speech and is neutral: "I live on my own."

blocks.title: Three traps for English speakers
items: "Each other" is never *sig*: *De ser varandra*, not *De ser sig* (= they see themselves).
*Sin* never stands inside the subject: *Hans fru och han…*, not *Sin fru och han…*
With *man*, use *sig* and *sin*, not *en* or *ens*, in standard Swedish: *Man ska ta hand om sig själv och sin familj.*

blocks.text: Swedes celebrate round birthdays — 30, 40, 50, 60 — and above all 50 — with surprising seriousness, often with speeches, songs written for the occasion and a long dinner. A *femtioårsdag* can be as big as a wedding. Golden weddings are rarer and even more of an event: three generations, a *smörgåstårta* (a savory sandwich cake) and at least one grandparent who "doesn't want any fuss".
Notice the family words: Swedish says exactly *whose* grandmother — *farmor* (father's mother), *mormor* (mother's mother), *farfar*, *morfar*. Oskar's *farmor* is his father's mother.

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Unit 4
items: Take three sentences from Unit 4 that contain an *att*-clause and add a possessive inside the subordinate clause. Ask yourself each time: who is the subject of *this* clause?
Example: *Dian säger att Oskar har glömt sin jacka* (Oskar's) vs *…att Oskar har glömt hennes jacka* (Dian's).
Then put the subordinate clause first: *Att Oskar hade glömt sin jacka märkte ingen.*
